title: Ecommerce design for a brand, not a marketplace
metaTitle: Ecommerce website design for brand shops
excerpt: A brand shop is an edited room with a point of view, not an infinite marketplace grid. Price, trust, and the path to pay still have to be obvious.
alt: A clothing shop interior with folded shirts, hanging jackets, shelves, and pendant lights. The room is edited and specific, which is the shape of a brand shop.

faqs.question: How is a brand shop different from a marketplace?
faqs.answer: A brand shop is an edited room: a point of view, short navigation, and products shown with consistent photographs. A marketplace is built for comparing listings. Copying that infinite grid throws away the reason to buy from this house.

faqs.question: Do shoppers still need plain facts in a designed shop?
faqs.answer: Price, materials, and the way to buy have to be findable. Baymard Institute's average of 50 studies, updated in 2025, puts the documented cart abandonment rate at 70.22%. The same research reports that 42% of US online shoppers have abandoned a cart because they were just browsing or not ready to buy, so the room has to be worth looking at.

faqs.question: What should a young brand shop postpone?
faqs.answer: Postpone a recommendation engine until a person can explain the pairing, a second visual system for a sale, and marketplace chrome you do not operate. A sale can be a banner with an end date. It should not introduce a new grid for a weekend.

markdown:
Ecommerce website design for brands is the design of an edited room. A visitor should feel which house they are in, see a small number of things chosen with a point of view, and find a way to look closer. A marketplace grid, infinite and neutral, answers a different question: which of these listings should I compare. A brand shop that copies that grid throws away the reason to buy here instead of anywhere.

The room can be quiet or loud. It cannot be undecided. Every extra module that says "you might also like" in a generic voice is the room leaking into a mall.

## Edit the room

Start with what this brand sells and what it refuses to look like. A clothing shop with a small collection wants the cloth, the cut, and the light to lead. A toolmaker wants the object and the job it does. Put those forward. Postpone the modules that exist so the page never has to choose: endless rows, a banner for every category, a popup that covers the thing you came to show.

Down the Cove is a public example of this kind of shop work: an ecommerce restructure, migration, and redesign, including a move off WooCommerce. No sales figure belongs in that sentence. The relevant fact is the kind of project. A brand catalog can be rebuilt as a shop with a point of view. Wabisabi is a different public example, a calm brand site, useful here as a reminder that restraint is a visual decision a visitor can feel. Neither project is a template to copy. Both show that a point of view can be built.

Edit means a sequence. The first screen names the house and shows the work. The next screen shows a few products or a few collections, with enough photograph to tell them apart. Deeper pages hold the rest. A person who wants everything can still get there. They should not be handed everything before they know where they are.

## What a brand shop still owes a shopper

Point of view is not an excuse for missing facts. Price, what the thing is made of, and how to buy it have to be findable. The edit is about order and emphasis. The facts are about not wasting the visit.

Baymard Institute, averaging 50 studies in a [list updated in 2025](https://baymard.com/lists/cart-abandonment-rate), calculates the documented online cart abandonment rate at 70.22%. The same write-up separates browsing from failure. It reports that 42% of US online shoppers have abandoned a cart because they were just browsing or not ready to buy. A brand room should be worth that visit. People who are not ready to purchase are still deciding whether this house is theirs. Treat the visit as time spent looking, which can become a purchase, and make the room good at being looked at.

The same research is a warning about trust and cost, which a designed room does not get to ignore. Shoppers also abandon because extra costs show up late, because they do not trust the site with payment, or because they are forced into an account. A beautiful collection with a surprise shipping fee, or a checkout that looks like a different company, undoes the room. Design the path from the edited collection to payment so it still feels like the same brand, and so the cost is visible before the last step.

The W3C's [Web Content Accessibility Guidelines](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) apply to the shop as well. Photographs need text alternatives. Buttons need names. The layout has to remain operable on a phone. A brand that is careful about crop and careless about focus has only designed the part a screenshot shows.

## Photography, type, and the grid you do use

When you do use a grid, give it rules. One crop, one background, one way of aligning type. Mixed crops and mixed backgrounds make even a small collection look unfinished, which reads as unfinished care. The grid is a wall in the room, not a dump of supplier images.

Type should sound like the brand in the product name, the short description, and the button. A poetic name with an "Add to cart" from a default theme is a small break, and small breaks add up to a shop that feels skinned rather than designed. Write the interface sentences with the same standard as the story at the top of the page.

Navigation should be short. A brand with twelve collections can show twelve. A brand with four should not invent twelve to look more serious. Categories are a promise that the things inside them belong together. If they do not, the room is a directory.

Hanabi's ecommerce work stays inside this idea: the shop is built, not only mocked, and the catalog remains something the team can keep true. Clarity over complexity applies to a product grid the same way it applies to a homepage.

## What to postpone

Postpone a recommendation engine until a person can explain why two products belong together better than the engine can. Until then, choose a few pairings by hand. A human pairing is a point of view. A random pairing is a marketplace habit.

Postpone a second visual system for sales events. A sale can be a banner with an end date. It should not introduce a new typeface and a new grid for a weekend. The room has to be recognizable on Monday.

Postpone marketplace features you do not operate: seller ratings, competing offers, a sort for "best match" that nobody on the team can define. If you do not have those facts, do not draw the chrome for them. Empty chrome is a promise of a marketplace you are not running, and shoppers will look for the comparison tools that are not there.

The next decision, once the room is edited, is the page where one object has to explain itself. That piece is [product pages that explain the thing, then step aside](/blog/product-pages-that-explain).

Selected brand and shop work lives with [Hanabi's work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works). The useful question in those projects is whether the shop still feels like one house.
